title: Imber. Nautes. Anchisae umbra
titleEn: The Rain on the Fleet, Nautes' Counsel, and Anchises' Vision — Aeneid V.680–778
part: The Rain on the Fleet, Nautes' Counsel, and Anchises' Vision (V.680–778)
about: The fire that Juno's frenzied women set to the ships will not die: it smoulders in the wet timber and creeps through the hulls, and the heroes' water does nothing. Aeneas tears off his cloak and prays to Jupiter, to spare the fleet or else to strike him down; at once a black storm breaks and drenches the ships, and all but four are saved. Shaken, he turns over whether to stay in Sicily or press on to Italy. Old Nautes, the one man Pallas has taught her arts, advises him: bear what fortune brings, leave the old, the weary and the faint-hearted with Acestes in a city to be called Acesta, and sail on with the bravest. That night his father Anchises comes down from heaven in a dream, sent by Jupiter, and tells him to follow Nautes's counsel, to fight down a hard people in Latium, and first to come to the Underworld by way of Avernus, guided by the Sibyl, where Anchises dwells in Elysium and will show him his race and the walls to come. Aeneas wakes and cannot catch him; he stirs the ashes and worships the Lar of Troy and Vesta. Then the city is marked out with a plough, houses are allotted, Acestes gives laws, a temple to Venus is founded on Eryx and a priest and grove for Anchises' tomb. After nine days' feasting the winds turn fair. The parting is full of tears, even from those who had hated the sea; Aeneas commends them to Acestes, sacrifices to Eryx and the Tempests, and, wreathed in olive, pours his offering into the waves from the prow. A following wind rises, and the crews bend to their oars.

sentences.t:
Sed non idcirco flammae atque incendia vires
indomitas posuere;
sentences.l:
But not on that account the flames and the fires their strength
untamed laid aside;
sentences.i: But the flames and the fires had not for all that laid aside their untamed strength;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, picking up the burning of the ships (the end of the last part). 'Idcirco' is 'on that account', 'for all that'. 'Vires indomitas posuere' is 'laid aside their untamed strength', 'posuere' a perfect in '-ere' for '-erunt' (you'll see this constantly). The Latin Library prints 'flamma… viris', 'flame… with strength', a different case-ending that would change the construction ('indomitas' needs 'vires' as its noun, which Greenough's text supplies).

sentences.t:
udo sub robore vivit
stuppa vomens tardum fumum, lentusque carinas
est vapor, et toto descendit corpore pestis,
nec vires heroum infusaque flumina prosunt.
sentences.l:
under the damp timber it lives, the tow,
spewing slow smoke, and sluggish on the keels
is the heat, and through the whole body descends the plague,
nor the strength of heroes and the poured waters avail.
sentences.i: Deep in the soaked timber the tow lives on, belching sluggish smoke; the heat clings slowly to the hulls, the plague works down through the whole frame, and neither the efforts of heroes nor the water they pour does any good.
sentences.n: 'Udo sub robore' is 'under the damp timber', 'robur' (properly oak) standing for ship's timber, a word you'll meet again. 'Stuppa' is 'tow', the fibre used to caulk a ship's seams, which smoulders inside the wet wood. 'Lentus… est vapor' is 'the heat is sluggish', and 'carinas' (the keels, the hulls) is a loose accusative after 'lentus', 'creeping slowly along the keels'; a poetic construction, and l gives the sense. 'Pestis' is 'plague', 'ruin', used of fire as of a sickness spreading through the 'corpus', the ship's body (the metaphor returns at 699, 'a peste'). 'Heroum' is the genitive plural of 'heros', 'hero'. 'Infusa… flumina' is 'poured-on streams', the water they throw on the fire; 'prosunt' (from 'prosum') is 'avail', with no dative expressed.

sentences.t:
Tum pius Aeneas umeris abscindere vestem,
auxilioque vocare deos, et tendere palmas:
sentences.l:
Then pious Aeneas from his shoulders to tear off his garment,
and to summon the gods to help, and to stretch out his palms:
sentences.i: Then pious Aeneas tore the cloak from his shoulders, called on the gods to help, and stretched out his palms:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Abscindere', 'vocare' and 'tendere' are historic infinitives, standing for imperfects ('he tore', 'he called', 'he stretched'), as with 'spectare' in the last part; they make the narrative quick. 'Pius' is Aeneas's constant epithet, and here the word to remember, for his prayer rests on it. 'Umeris' is a dative or ablative of separation, 'from his shoulders'; 'auxilio' is a dative of purpose, 'for help'. Palms held up are the ancient posture of prayer. The colon leads to the prayer.

sentences.t:
“Iuppiter omnipotens, si nondum exosus ad unum
Troianos, si quid pietas antiqua labores
respicit humanos, da flammam evadere classi
nunc, Pater, et tenues Teucrum res eripe leto.
sentences.l:
“Jupiter almighty, if not yet hating to the last one
the Trojans, if anything of piety of old the toils
of men regards, grant, the flame to escape, to the fleet
now, Father, and the slender fortunes of the Teucrians snatch from death.
sentences.i: “Almighty Jupiter, if you have not yet come to hate the Trojans down to the last of them, if any old compassion regards the labours of men, grant that the fleet escape the flame now, Father, and snatch the Teucrians' slender fortunes from death.
sentences.n: The opening mark begins Aeneas's prayer, which runs to 692. 'Si nondum exosus ad unum Troianos' is 'if not yet hating the Trojans to the last one': 'exosus' is the perfect participle of the defective verb 'exodi' (the perfect-form verb 'hate utterly'), with an active sense, 'having come to hate', and 'ad unum' 'down to one', 'to a man'. 'Si quid pietas antiqua labores respicit humanos' is 'if any ancient piety (or pity) regards human toils', 'si quid' is 'if at all', 'if in any degree' (the 'quid' is adverbial). Whose piety it is is left open: Jupiter's old compassion, or the old devotion of the Trojans. 'Da… evadere' is 'grant to escape', 'do' with a bare infinitive, a poetic construction. 'Teucrum' is the old genitive plural in '-um' (you'll see this constantly). 'Tenues… res' are 'slender fortunes', the little that remains. 'Eripe leto' is 'snatch from death', 'leto' an ablative of separation. The Latin Library prints 'tenuis', the same accusative plural in another spelling.

sentences.t:
Vel tu, quod superest infesto fulmine morti,
si mereor, demitte, tuaque hic obrue dextra.”
sentences.l:
Or you, what is left, with hostile thunderbolt, to death,
if I deserve it, send down, and with your right hand overwhelm, here.”
sentences.i: Or else, if I deserve it, send down to death whatever is left of us with your angry bolt, and overwhelm us here with your own right hand.”
sentences.n: 'Vel' sets the second choice against the first: save the fleet, or finish us. 'Tu' is emphatic, 'you yourself'. 'Quod superest' is 'what remains', a neuter relative for the survivors ('morti' is a dative, 'to death'), with 'infesto fulmine' 'with hostile thunderbolt'. 'Si mereor' is 'if I deserve it', a bare, plain 'if'. 'Demitte' (from 'demitto', 'send down') and 'obrue' ('overwhelm') are singular imperatives; both take 'quod superest' as their object, and 'tua… dextra' is an ablative of means. 'Hic' is 'here', on the spot. The closing mark ends the prayer.

sentences.i: Hardly had he spoken when a black storm broke in streaming rain, raged beyond all measure, and the high places of the earth and the plains shook with thunder;
sentences.n: 'Vix… cum' is the inverted 'cum' pattern, 'scarcely… when', with the pluperfect 'ediderat' for what had barely finished and the present for the sudden answer. 'Effusis imbribus' is an ablative of manner, 'with pouring rains'. 'Atra tempestas' is the 'black storm'; 'sine more' is 'without restraint', 'beyond measure'. 'Tonitru' is an ablative of cause (fourth declension), 'with thunder'. 'Ardua terrarum' is a neuter plural adjective with a partitive genitive, 'the steep (places) of the lands'; the high ground and the 'campi', 'plains', shake together. The prayer is answered at once, a sign of the god's favour.

sentences.t:
ruit aethere toto
turbidus imber aqua densisque nigerrimus austris;
sentences.l:
rushes from the whole sky
murky the rain with water and, by thick south winds, blackest;
sentences.i: a murky deluge pours from the whole sky, heavy with water and blackest with the crowding southern gales;
sentences.n: 'Ruit' is 'comes rushing down', and 'aethere toto' 'from the whole upper air', an ablative of separation. 'Turbidus imber' is a 'murky downpour'; 'aqua' is an ablative of means, 'with water'. 'Densis… austris' is 'with thick south winds', 'austris' a plural for the wind, an ablative of means, with 'nigerrimus' (the superlative of 'niger', 'black') agreeing with 'imber', 'blackest'. The 'Auster' is the south wind, the rain-bringing wind of Italy and Sicily.

sentences.t: implenturque super puppes;
sentences.l: and are filled, from above, the sterns;
sentences.i: the sterns fill with water from above;
sentences.n: 'Implentur' is passive, 'are filled', with 'puppes' as subject: 'puppis', the stern, stands for the whole ship (part for whole), and 'super' is an adverb, 'from above'. The enclitic '-que' joins this short clause to the last.

sentences.t:
semiusta madescunt
robora;
sentences.l:
half-burnt are soaked
the timbers;
sentences.i: the half-burnt timbers are drenched;
sentences.n: 'Semiusta' is 'half-burnt' (Greenough's form; the Latin Library prints 'semusta', a shorter spelling of the same word, from 'semi-ustus', from 'uro', 'burn'). 'Madescunt' is an inchoative in '-sco', 'become wet', 'are soaked'. 'Robora', 'timbers', is the word of 681, 'robur', in the plural.

sentences.t:
restinctus donec vapor omnis, et omnes,
quattuor amissis, servatae a peste carinae.
sentences.l:
until quenched the heat all, and all,
four having been lost, saved from the plague the keels.
sentences.i: until all the heat was quenched, and all the hulls, bar the four that were lost, were saved from the plague.
sentences.n: 'Donec' is 'until', and 'restinctus… vapor omnis' is 'all the heat quenched', with 'est' left out, as with 'servatae (sunt)'. 'Omnes… carinae' is 'all the keels', 'omnes' split from its noun across the line, with 'quattuor amissis' an ablative absolute, 'four having been lost'. 'A peste' is 'from the plague', the 'pestis' of 683, the fire that spread like a sickness. Four ships are lost, a number to remember.

sentences.t:
At pater Aeneas, casu concussus acerbo,
nunc huc ingentes, nunc illuc pectore curas
mutabat versans, Siculisne resideret arvis,
oblitus fatorum, Italasne capesseret oras.
sentences.l:
But father Aeneas, by the bitter chance shaken,
now hither, now thither, in his breast, mighty cares
was shifting, turning over — whether in Sicilian fields he should settle,
forgetful of the fates, or the Italian shores should seize.
sentences.i: But father Aeneas, shaken by the bitter blow, turned vast anxieties this way and that in his breast, weighing whether to settle on Sicilian fields, forgetting the fates, or to make for the shores of Italy.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Pater' is a title of respect, the commander as father of his people. 'Casu concussus acerbo' is 'shaken by the bitter chance', 'casu' an ablative of cause. 'Nunc huc… nunc illuc' is 'now this way, now that', framing 'ingentes… curas', 'mighty cares', as objects of 'mutabat versans', 'was shifting, turning over', the verb and its participle saying the same thing twice, for restlessness. 'Siculisne… Italasne' is the double question 'whether… or' with '-ne… -ne', and 'resideret' and 'capesseret' are imperfect subjunctives in an indirect question. 'Capesseret' is an intensive form of 'capio', 'take eagerly', 'make for'. 'Oblitus fatorum' is a perfect participle with the genitive: to stay would be to forget the fates (the promise of Italy). The Latin Library prints 'ingentis', the same accusative plural spelled with '-is'.

sentences.t:
Tum senior Nautes, unum Tritonia Pallas
quem docuit multaque insignem reddidit arte,
haec responsa dabat, vel quae portenderet ira
magna deum, vel quae fatorum posceret ordo;
sentences.l:
Then the elder Nautes, whom alone Tritonian Pallas
had taught and rendered distinguished with much art,
these replies was giving, either what might portend the wrath
great of the gods, or what the order of the fates might demand;
sentences.i: Then aged Nautes, the one man whom Tritonian Pallas had taught and made renowned for his great skill, was giving answers, such as the great wrath of the gods foretold or the order of the fates required;
sentences.n: 'Nautes' is an old Trojan counsellor; later tradition made him the ancestor of the Roman family of the Nautii, said to have kept a cult of Pallas (this comes from the ancient commentators, not from Virgil). 'Unum… quem' is 'him alone whom', 'unum' a predicative accusative: Pallas had taught him alone. 'Tritonia Pallas' is Athena, 'Tritonia' one of her epithets (a title of uncertain origin, which the ancients derived from a Lake or River Triton where she was said to have been born). 'Docuit' and 'reddidit' are perfects, and 'multa… arte' an ablative of means. 'Responsa dabat' is 'was giving answers', the imperfect for his habit of advising. 'Vel quae portenderet… vel quae… posceret' is a double indirect question, 'either what… portended, or what… demanded', with imperfect subjunctives. 'Deum' is the old genitive plural in '-um' (you'll see this constantly), 'of the gods'.

sentences.t: isque his Aenean solatus vocibus infit:
sentences.l: and he, with these words Aeneas consoling, begins:
sentences.i: and he, comforting Aeneas, began with these words:
sentences.n: 'Isque' is 'et is', 'and he'. 'Solatus' is a perfect participle of the deponent 'solor', 'having consoled', 'consoling', with an active sense. 'Infit' is a defective verb, found only in a few forms, 'begins (to speak)', an archaism; it governs the speech after the colon.

sentences.t: “Nate dea, quo fata trahunt retrahuntque, sequamur;
sentences.l: “Goddess-born, whither the fates draw and draw back, let us follow;
sentences.i: “Son of a goddess, let us follow wherever the fates lead on or draw back;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the beginning of Nautes's speech, which runs to 718. 'Nate dea' is 'son born of a goddess', 'nate' a vocative ('son') and 'dea' an ablative of origin; his mother is Venus. 'Quo fata trahunt retrahuntque' is 'where the fates draw and draw back', 'retrahunt' the compound that adds the opposite pull, 'to and fro' for advance or setback. 'Sequamur' is a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us follow'.

sentences.t: quidquid erit, superanda omnis fortuna ferendo est.
sentences.l: whatever it shall be, to be overcome all fortune by bearing is.
sentences.i: whatever shall come, every turn of fortune must be mastered by endurance.
sentences.n: 'Quidquid erit' is 'whatever will be', a complete future clause with 'quidquid' for 'quicquid'. 'Superanda… est' is the passive periphrastic, 'is to be overcome', 'must be overcome', with 'omnis… fortuna' as subject and 'ferendo' an ablative of the gerund, 'by bearing', 'by endurance': a maxim in five words.

sentences.t: Est tibi Dardanius divinae stirpis Acestes:
sentences.l: There is to you Dardanian of divine stock Acestes:
sentences.i: You have Acestes, a Trojan by descent and of divine stock:
sentences.n: 'Est tibi' is a dative of possession, 'you have' (you'll see this constantly), the thing possessed 'Acestes' set at the end. 'Dardanius' is 'of Dardanus's line', 'Trojan': Acestes's mother was a Trojan woman (told at the start of Book V). 'Divinae stirpis' is a genitive of quality, 'of divine stock', his father being a river-god. The colon leads on to what Aeneas is to do with him.

sentences.t: hunc cape consiliis socium et coniunge volentem;
sentences.l: him take as ally into your counsels and join, willing;
sentences.i: take him into your counsels as an ally, and join him to you, for he is willing;
sentences.n: 'Hunc cape… socium' is 'take him as ally', 'socium' a predicative accusative, and 'consiliis' a dative, 'for your counsels', 'into your plans'. 'Coniunge' is the imperative of 'coniungo', 'join (to you)'. 'Volentem' is a present participle agreeing with 'hunc', 'willing', 'since he is willing'.

sentences.t:
huic trade, amissis superant qui navibus, et quos
pertaesum magni incepti rerumque tuarum est;
sentences.l:
to him hand over those who survive, the ships being lost, and those whom
it has thoroughly wearied of the great undertaking and of your affairs;
sentences.i: To him hand over those who are left, now that the ships are lost, and those who have grown weary of the great enterprise and of your cause;
sentences.n: 'Huic trade' is 'hand over to him', 'huic' a dative. 'Amissis… navibus' is an ablative absolute, 'the ships having been lost'; 'superant… qui' is 'those who survive' ('supero' in its sense 'remain over'). 'Quos pertaesum… est' is the impersonal 'pertaedet', 'it wearies thoroughly', with the accusative of the person ('quos') and the genitives of the thing: 'magni incepti', 'of the great undertaking' ('inceptum', a perfect participle used as a noun), and 'rerum tuarum', 'of your affairs', 'of your cause'. These are the ones too weary to go on.

sentences.t:
longaevosque senes ac fessas aequore matres,
et quidquid tecum invalidum metuensque pericli est,
delige, et his habeant terris sine moenia fessi:
sentences.l:
and the long-lived old men and the mothers weary with the sea,
and whatever with you is weak and fearful of danger,
choose out, and in these lands allow them to have walls, the weary:
sentences.i: Pick out the aged men and the mothers worn out by the sea, and all in your company who are weak and afraid of danger, and let the weary have walls in these lands:
sentences.n: 'Longaevos… senes' are 'long-lived old men', 'fessas aequore matres' 'mothers weary from the sea' ('aequore' an ablative of cause). 'Quidquid tecum invalidum metuensque pericli est' is 'whatever is weak with you and fearful of danger': 'quidquid' is neuter, so it covers anyone and anything, 'metuens' takes the genitive 'pericli', a syncopated form of 'periculi', Virgil's usual shortening. 'Delige' is the imperative of 'deligo', 'choose out', and governs all three. 'Sine' is the imperative of 'sino', 'allow', followed by 'habeant', a subjunctive without 'ut' ('allow that they have'); 'his… terris' is 'in these lands', and 'fessi' is the subject, the weary, left at the end.

sentences.t: urbem appellabunt permisso nomine Acestam.”
sentences.l: a city they will call, the name permitted, Acesta.”
sentences.i: and, with your leave on the name, they shall call the city Acesta.”
sentences.n: 'Urbem appellabunt' is 'they will name the city', with 'Acestam' a second accusative, the name given to the city ('call the city Acesta'); 'Acestam' is the ordinary first-declension accusative of 'Acesta'. 'Permisso nomine' is an ablative absolute, 'the name being permitted', that is, with Aeneas's leave and with Acestes honoured by the name; this city was later identified with Segesta (Egesta) in Sicily. The closing mark ends Nautes's speech.

sentences.t:
Talibus incensus dictis senioris amici,
tum vero in curas animo diducitur omnes.
sentences.l:
By such words kindled of an elder friend,
then indeed into cares in his mind he is torn apart, all.
sentences.i: Stirred by this speech from his aged friend, he was now pulled apart in mind among all his cares.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Talibus incensus dictis' is 'kindled by such words', 'incensus' the perfect participle passive of 'incendo', and 'senioris amici' a genitive with 'dictis', 'of his elder friend'. 'Tum vero' is 'then indeed', marking the effect. 'Diducitur' is the present passive of 'diduco', 'is drawn apart': he was pulled this way and that by his cares even more than before. 'Animo' is an ablative of respect, 'in his mind'; 'in curas… omnes' is 'into all his cares'. The Latin Library prints 'omnis', the same accusative plural in another spelling.

sentences.t: Et nox atra polum bigis subvecta tenebat:
sentences.l: And night, black, the sky on her two-horse chariot borne up, held:
sentences.i: And dark Night, borne up on her chariot, held the heavens:
sentences.n: 'Nox atra' is 'black night', and 'bigis' an ablative of means, 'on a two-horse chariot', the common picture of Night driving across the sky. 'Subvecta' is the perfect participle passive of 'subveho', 'carried up', 'borne up' (on her chariot). 'Polum… tenebat' is 'held the vault of heaven', 'polus' the sky. The colon introduces the vision.

sentences.t:
visa dehinc caelo facies delapsa parentis
Anchisae subito tales effundere voces:
sentences.l:
seemed, then, from heaven, the appearance, slipped down, of his father
Anchises suddenly such to pour forth words:
sentences.i: then the form of his father Anchises seemed to glide down from heaven and suddenly pour out such words:
sentences.n: 'Visa… facies… effundere' is 'the form seemed to pour out', 'visa' (with 'est' left out) a perfect passive of 'video' in the sense 'seemed', with the infinitive. 'Facies' is the appearance, 'shape', here a dream-image; 'delapsa' is the perfect participle of 'delabor', 'slipped down', and 'caelo' an ablative of separation, 'from the sky'. 'Parentis Anchisae' is 'of his parent Anchises', the genitive 'parentis' set before the name. 'Tales… voces' is 'such words'; the Latin Library prints 'talis', the same accusative plural in another spelling. The colon leads to Anchises's speech.

sentences.t:
“Nate, mihi vita quondam, dum vita manebat,
care magis, nate, Iliacis exercite fatis,
imperio Iovis huc venio, qui classibus ignem
depulit, et caelo tandem miseratus ab alto est.
sentences.l:
“Son, to me than life once, while life remained,
dearer, son, harried by Ilian fates,
by Jove's command I come here, who from your fleet the fire
drove off, and from heaven at last has pitied from on high.
sentences.i: “My son, once dearer to me than life itself, while life remained, my son, tried by the fates of Ilium, I come at Jove's command, who has driven the fire from your ships and has at last taken pity from high heaven.
sentences.n: The opening mark begins Anchises's speech, which runs to 739. 'Mihi vita quondam… care magis' is 'dearer to me than life once', with 'vita' an ablative of comparison. 'Dum vita manebat' is 'while life remained', 'dum' with the imperfect indicative. 'Nate' is repeated, a tender double address. 'Exercite' is a vocative, the perfect participle of 'exerceo', 'harassed', 'worn down', 'Iliacis fatis' 'by the fates of Ilium'. 'Imperio Iovis' is an ablative of cause, 'by Jove's order'; 'qui' is the relative, 'he who', with 'classibus' a dative of separation, 'from the fleets'. 'Depulit' is 'drove off'. 'Miseratus… est' is the perfect of the deponent 'miseror', 'has pitied', with 'est' held back to the end of the line, after 'caelo tandem… ab alto'; 'caelo… ab alto' is 'from high heaven'. There is no tmesis here. The sense is that Jupiter heard the prayer of 687–692.

sentences.t:
Consiliis pare, quae nunc pulcherrima Nautes
dat senior;
sentences.l:
To counsels give heed, which now the best Nautes
gives, the elder;
sentences.i: Heed the counsel that old Nautes now gives, the best that could be given;
sentences.n: 'Consiliis pare' is 'obey the counsels', 'pare' the imperative of 'pareo', which takes the dative. 'Quae nunc pulcherrima… dat' is 'which, the finest, he now gives', 'pulcherrima' a superlative agreeing with 'quae', 'most excellent'. 'Senior' is 'the elder', 'the old man', in apposition to 'Nautes'. The ghost thereby endorses what Nautes said.

sentences.t:
lectos iuvenes, fortissima corda,
defer in Italiam;
sentences.l:
chosen young men, the bravest hearts,
carry to Italy;
sentences.i: carry to Italy the chosen young men, the bravest hearts;
sentences.n: 'Lectos iuvenes' are 'chosen young men', objects of 'defer', 'carry down', 'bring' (the imperative of 'defero'). 'Fortissima corda' is an apposition in the neuter plural to masculine nouns ('hearts' for brave spirits, a construction by sense), 'the bravest hearts'.

sentences.t:
gens dura atque aspera cultu
debellanda tibi Latio est.
sentences.l:
a race hard and rough in way of life
is to be conquered by you in Latium.
sentences.i: In Latium you must fight down a race hard and rough in its ways.
sentences.n: 'Gens dura atque aspera cultu' is 'a race hard and rough in its manner of life', 'cultu' an ablative of respect. 'Debellanda tibi… est' is a passive periphrastic with a dative of the agent, 'is to be fought to the finish by you', 'debello' with 'de-' as an intensive, 'fight down'. 'Latio' is an ablative of place, 'in Latium'; the hard people are the Latins and Rutulians of the later books.

sentences.t:
Ditis tamen ante
infernas accede domos, et Averna per alta
congressus pete, nate, meos.
sentences.l:
Of Dis, however, before that
the infernal approach houses, and through Avernian deeps
seek meetings, son, mine.
sentences.i: But before that, go to the infernal home of Dis, and through the deep places of Avernus seek out a meeting with me, my son.
sentences.n: 'Ditis' is the genitive of 'Dis', the king of the dead, Pluto. 'Ante' is an adverb, 'first', 'before that', with 'tamen', 'nevertheless': the founding in Latium has to wait for a journey below. 'Accede' is the imperative of 'accedo', 'approach', with the accusative 'infernas… domos', 'the houses below'. 'Averna per alta' is 'through the deep places of Avernus', 'Averna… alta' neuter plural adjectives agreeing with each other (the Avernian deeps), 'per' placed after its adjective: the lake Avernus near Cumae was one entrance to the Underworld. 'Congressus' is a fourth-declension accusative plural, 'meetings', and 'pete… meos' is 'seek my meetings', that is, 'come and meet me'.

sentences.t:
Non me impia namque
Tartara habent, tristes umbrae, sed amoena piorum
concilia Elysiumque colo.
sentences.l:
Not me impious
Tartarus holds, sad shades, but pleasant, of the pious
assemblies and Elysium I inhabit.
sentences.i: For it is not the impious realm of Tartarus, the home of gloomy shades, that holds me; I dwell in the pleasant company of the pious and in Elysium.
sentences.n: 'Namque' is 'for', set after its first words. 'Impia Tartara' is 'impious Tartarus', neuter plural, 'impia' a transferred epithet: Tartarus is where the impious are held. 'Tristes umbrae' is 'the sad shades', a phrase in apposition to what 'Tartara' holds. 'Amoena piorum concilia' is 'the pleasant assemblies of the pious', 'concilia' (with 'Elysium') the objects of 'colo', 'I dwell in', 'I haunt'. Elysium is the Blessed's abode.

sentences.t:
Huc casta Sibylla
nigrarum multo pecudum te sanguine ducet:
sentences.l:
Hither the chaste Sibyl
of black cattle with much blood will lead you:
sentences.i: Hither the chaste Sibyl will lead you, once the blood of many black cattle has flowed:
sentences.n: 'Huc' is 'hither', to Elysium. 'Casta Sibylla' is 'the chaste Sibyl', the virgin prophetess of Cumae, priestess of Apollo, who will be Aeneas's guide in Book VI. 'Nigrarum multo pecudum sanguine' is 'with the blood of many black beasts', an ablative of means: black victims were offered to the powers of the Underworld. The colon leads on to what he will learn there.

sentences.t: tum genus omne tuum, et quae dentur moenia, disces.
sentences.l: then your whole race, and what walls may be given, you will learn.
sentences.i: Then you will learn the whole of your line, and what walls are to be granted you.
sentences.n: 'Genus omne tuum' is 'your whole race', your descendants. 'Quae dentur moenia' is an indirect question, 'what walls are to be given', 'dentur' a present subjunctive. 'Disces' is the future of 'disco'. This promises the parade of Rome's future heroes in VI.

sentences.t: Iamque vale:
sentences.l: And now farewell:
sentences.i: And now farewell:
sentences.n: 'Iamque vale' is 'and now farewell', 'vale' the imperative of 'valeo', the ordinary Latin goodbye; the colon leads to the reason, that the night is passing and he must go. The ghost's visit is short.

sentences.t:
torquet medios Nox humida cursus,
et me saevus equis Oriens adflavit anhelis.”
sentences.l:
turns the middle courses Night, dewy,
and me the cruel Orient with panting horses has breathed upon.”
sentences.i: dewy Night is turning through the middle of her course, and the cruel East has breathed on me with the panting horses of the dawn.”
sentences.n: 'Torquet medios… cursus' is 'turns her middle course', 'medios' agreeing with 'cursus': Night is at her half-way point and driving down. 'Humida' is 'moist', 'dewy' (the Latin Library prints it without the 'h', 'umida'). 'Me… adflavit' is 'has breathed upon me', 'adflavit' Greenough's spelling of 'afflavit', 'equis… anhelis' an ablative of means, 'with panting horses': the dawn's horses breathe on him, a sign that the shades must go back before daybreak. 'Saevus Oriens' is 'the cruel East'. The closing mark ends Anchises's speech.

sentences.t: Dixerat, et tenuis fugit, ceu fumus, in auras.
sentences.l: He had spoken, and thin fled, like smoke, into the breezes.
sentences.i: He had spoken, and, thin as smoke, he fled into the air.
sentences.n: 'Dixerat' is a pluperfect, the usual Virgilian way of ending a speech, 'he had spoken'. 'Tenuis' is a masculine nominative singular adjective, 'thin', 'airy', agreeing with the ghost (with 'fugit', 'fled'). 'Ceu fumus' is 'like smoke', 'ceu' a poetic 'as'. 'In auras' is 'into the breezes', 'into thin air'. The dream-father vanishes as Creusa's ghost did in Book II.

sentences.t:
Aeneas, “Quo deinde ruis, quo proripis? ”inquit,
“Quem fugis, aut quis te nostris complexibus arcet?”
sentences.l:
Aeneas: “Where then do you rush, where do you hurry off?” he says,
“Whom do you flee, or who from our embraces bars you?”
sentences.i: Aeneas: “Where do you rush off to now, where do you tear yourself away?” he cried; “whom do you flee, or who keeps you from our embrace?”
sentences.n: The print has 'proripis? ”inquit,', the closing mark of Aeneas's first cry set after the space and joined to 'inquit', a misprint for 'proripis?” inquit,'; t keeps the print, and l and i close the cry after 'proripis?'. The second cry has its own opening mark at 742. 'Aeneas' is the subject of an understood 'inquit', with 'inquit' placed after the speech. 'Quo deinde ruis, quo proripis' is 'where then are you rushing, where tearing yourself away?', 'proripis' a reflexive use of 'proripio' with 'te' left out, and 'quo' repeated. 'Quem fugis' is 'whom do you flee?', 'quis… arcet' 'who keeps you off', 'nostris complexibus' an ablative of separation, 'from our embraces'. The failed embrace recalls Aeneas's three attempts to hold Creusa's ghost (II.792–794) and, behind them, Homer's scenes in which a living man cannot hold a ghost (the Iliad's Patroclus, the Odyssey's mother of Odysseus).

sentences.t:
Haec memorans cinerem et sopitos suscitat ignes,
Pergameumque Larem et canae penetralia Vestae
farre pio et plena supplex veneratur acerra.
sentences.l:
These things speaking, the ashes and the sleeping fires he stirs up,
and the Pergamean Lar and of hoary Vesta the inner shrine
with pious meal and a full incense-box, suppliant, he worships.
sentences.i: With these words he rouses the ashes and the drowsy embers, and, as a suppliant, worships the Lar of Pergamum and the inner shrine of white-haired Vesta with sacred meal and a brimming box of incense.
sentences.n: 'Haec memorans' is 'saying these things', 'memorans' from 'memoro', 'speak of'. 'Cinerem et sopitos… ignes' are 'the ash and the sleeping fires', the embers of a hearth that he rouses to make an offering (the Latin Library prints 'ignis', the same accusative plural in another spelling). 'Pergameum Larem' is 'the Lar of Pergamum', the household god of Troy (Pergamum is Troy's citadel); 'canae penetralia Vestae' is 'the inner shrine of hoary Vesta', 'penetralia' a neuter plural for the innermost part of a temple or house, and Vesta the goddess of the hearth, whose fire Aeneas brought from Troy. 'Farre pio et plena… acerra' is 'with pious meal and a full incense-box', two ablatives of means: 'far' is the coarse spelt-meal for offerings. 'Supplex' is 'as a suppliant', predicative, and 'veneratur' a deponent, 'worships'.

sentences.t:
Extemplo socios primumque arcessit Acesten,
et Iovis imperium et cari praecepta parentis
edocet, et quae nunc animo sententia constet.
sentences.l:
Immediately his comrades and first Acestes he summons,
and of Jove the command and of his dear father the precepts
he teaches fully, and what now in his mind the decision stands.
sentences.i: At once he summons his comrades, and Acestes first of all, and tells them fully of the command of Jupiter, the precepts of his dear father, and what resolve is now fixed in his mind.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Extemplo' is 'at once'. 'Arcessit' is 'summons', Greenough's spelling (the Latin Library prints 'accersit', the same word). 'Primum… Acesten' is 'Acestes first', 'Acesten' a Greek accusative. 'Edocet' is 'teaches thoroughly', 'tells in full', and takes three objects: 'imperium', 'praecepta' and an indirect question, 'quae… sententia constet', 'what decision stands firm', 'constet' a present subjunctive. 'Animo' is a dative or ablative with 'constet', 'in his mind'. Note that Aeneas tells them of the command of Jupiter as well as the precepts of Anchises, as Anchises had commanded at 726–727.

sentences.t: Haud mora consiliis, nec iussa recusat Acestes.
sentences.l: No delay to the counsels, nor the orders refuses Acestes.
sentences.i: There is no delay in carrying out the plan, and Acestes does not refuse the orders.
sentences.n: 'Haud mora' is 'no delay', with 'est' left out, and 'consiliis' a dative, 'to the counsels', 'as to the plans'. 'Iussa' is a neuter plural, 'the orders', a perfect participle used as a noun; 'recusat' is 'refuses'. Acestes agrees at once.

sentences.t:
Transcribunt urbi matres, populumque volentem
deponunt, animos nil magnae laudis egentes.
sentences.l:
They transcribe to the city the mothers, and the people willing
they set down, spirits nothing of great praise needing.
sentences.i: They enrol the mothers in the new city, and settle the willing people there, souls that have no need of great renown.
sentences.n: 'Transcribunt' is 'enrol', 'transfer', from 'transcribo', 'write over', used of entering names on the roll of a new city, with 'urbi' a dative. 'Populum volentem deponunt' is 'they set down the willing people', 'deponunt' 'leave behind'. 'Animos… egentes' is an accusative apposition to the people, 'spirits needing nothing of great praise', 'egeo' taking the genitive 'laudis', and 'nil' an accusative of the extent: these are the weary, who want no heroism. The Latin Library prints 'egentis', the same accusative plural in another spelling.

sentences.t:
Ipsi transtra novant, flammisque ambesa reponunt
robora navigiis, aptant remosque rudentesque,
exigui numero, sed bello vivida virtus.
sentences.l:
They themselves the benches renew, and by flames gnawed they replace
timbers in the ships, and fit oars and ropes,
few in number, but in war lively valour.
sentences.i: They themselves renew the benches and replace for the ships the timbers the flames had gnawed, and fit oars and ropes, few in number, but their courage alive for war.
sentences.n: 'Ipsi' is 'they themselves', the Trojan crews who go on. 'Transtra novant' is 'renew the benches', the rowers' cross-seats. 'Flammisque ambesa… robora' is 'timbers gnawed round by flames', 'ambesa' the perfect participle passive of 'ambedo', 'eat around', 'flammis' an ablative of means; 'reponunt… navigiis' is 'put back for the vessels', 'navigiis' a dative ('navigium', 'vessel'). 'Aptant' is 'fit out'. 'Rudentes' are 'ropes', rigging (the Latin Library prints 'rudentisque', the same accusative plural). 'Exigui numero' is 'small in number', 'numero' an ablative of respect, nominative plural with 'ipsi'; 'bello vivida virtus' is 'their valour lively for war', 'est' left out: the picked few have the strength of many.

sentences.t:
Interea Aeneas urbem designat aratro
sortiturque domos;
sentences.l:
Meanwhile Aeneas the city marks out with the plough
and allots the homes;
sentences.i: Meanwhile Aeneas marks out the city with a plough and allots the homesteads;
sentences.n: 'Urbem designat aratro' is 'marks out the city with the plough', 'aratro' an ablative of means: the Roman rite of founding a city, by ploughing a furrow around the walls' line. 'Sortitur… domos' is 'allots by lot the dwellings', 'sortior' a deponent, 'domos' an accusative plural.

sentences.t:
hoc Ilium et haec loca Troiam
esse iubet.
sentences.l:
this Ilium and these places Troy
to be he bids.
sentences.i: Here, he decrees, shall be Ilium, and this land Troy.
sentences.n: 'Hoc Ilium et haec loca Troiam esse iubet' is an accusative and infinitive after 'iubet', 'he orders this (place) to be Ilium and these places Troy', 'Ilium' (neuter) is the town, and 'haec loca Troiam' 'this district Troy' (the ancient commentators take Ilium as the city and Troia as the land round it). As at III.349–351, new names for old.

sentences.t:
Gaudet regno Troianus Acestes,
indicitque forum et patribus dat iura vocatis.
sentences.l:
Rejoices in the kingdom the Trojan Acestes,
and proclaims a forum and gives laws to the senators summoned.
sentences.i: Trojan Acestes rejoices in his new realm, appoints a forum, and gives laws to the fathers he has summoned.
sentences.n: 'Gaudet regno' is 'rejoices in the kingdom', 'regno' an ablative of cause, as 'gaudeo' often takes. 'Troianus Acestes' is 'Trojan Acestes', as 'Dardanius' at 711. 'Indicit forum' is 'proclaims a forum', 'sets up an assembly and court' ('forum indicere' is the Roman phrase for announcing a sitting), and 'patribus… vocatis' is 'to the fathers called together', 'patres' the senators, 'vocatis' a perfect participle passive. The Roman words ('forum', 'patres', 'iura') make the new town a small Rome.

sentences.t:
Tum vicina astris, Erycino in vertice sedes
fundatur Veneri Idaliae, tumuloque sacerdos
ac lucus late sacer additur Anchiseo.
sentences.l:
Then near to the stars, on Eryx's summit, a seat
is founded for Idalian Venus, and to the tomb a priest
and a grove far and wide sacred is added, Anchisean.
sentences.i: Then, close to the stars, on the summit of Eryx a shrine is founded for Idalian Venus, and a priest and a grove, sacred for a great distance round, are added to Anchises' tomb.
sentences.n: 'Tum' is 'then'. 'Vicina astris' is 'neighbouring the stars', 'vicina' with a dative, agreeing with 'sedes', and 'Erycino in vertice' 'on the Erycine peak', 'Erycinus' the adjective of Mount Eryx, in western Sicily. 'Sedes fundatur' is 'a seat (a temple) is founded', for 'Veneri Idaliae', 'Idalian Venus', named from Idalium in Cyprus, where she was worshipped. 'Tumulo… Anchiseo' is a dative, 'to the Anchisean tomb', the adjective standing for the genitive. 'Sacerdos ac lucus' make a double subject, with the singular verb 'additur' agreeing with the nearer ('lucus late sacer'). The Latin Library prints 'additus', a participle, so that the clause would run on with 'est' understood; the sense is the same.

sentences.t:
Iamque dies epulata novem gens omnis, et aris
factus honos:
sentences.l:
And now days having feasted nine the people all, and on the altars
honour has been done:
sentences.i: Now the whole people had feasted for nine days, and honour had been paid at the altars:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Iamque' is 'and now'. 'Dies epulata novem gens omnis' is 'the whole people having feasted nine days', 'epulata' the perfect participle of the deponent 'epulor' with an active sense, 'dies novem' an accusative of duration: the nine days recall the Roman 'novendiale', the nine-day rites after a death. 'Aris factus honos' is 'honour done at the altars', 'est' left out, 'honos' the sacrifice.

sentences.t:
placidi straverunt aequora venti,
creber et adspirans rursus vocat Auster in altum.
sentences.l:
gentle have levelled the seas the winds,
and thick and breathing again calls the South wind into the deep.
sentences.i: the gentle winds have smoothed the water, and the South wind, blowing steadily once more, calls them out to the open sea.
sentences.n: 'Placidi straverunt aequora venti' is 'the calm winds have levelled the seas', 'straverunt' the full perfect ending '-erunt' (the shorter '-ere' is not used here). 'Creber' is 'thick', 'frequent', a steady wind, with 'adspirans' (the Latin Library prints it 'aspirans'), 'blowing on' (them). 'Auster' is the south wind, and 'in altum' 'into the deep sea', 'altum' a neuter noun for the open sea. 'Rursus' is 'again'.

sentences.t: Exoritur procurva ingens per litora fletus;
sentences.l: Arises along the curved shores a huge wailing;
sentences.i: A great wailing rises all along the curving shore;
sentences.n: 'Exoritur' is 'arises', 'procurva… per litora' 'along the curving shores', 'procurvus' meaning 'bending forward' (a bay). 'Ingens fletus' is 'a great weeping', a fourth-declension noun.

sentences.t: complexi inter se noctemque diemque morantur.
sentences.l: embraced among themselves, night and day they linger.
sentences.i: Locked in each other's arms they linger night and day.
sentences.n: 'Complexi' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'complector', 'having embraced', with an active sense. 'Inter se' is 'one another'. 'Noctemque diemque' is a double '-que', 'both night and day', an accusative of duration, and 'morantur' 'they linger', 'delay'.

sentences.t:
Ipsae iam matres, ipsi, quibus aspera quondam
visa maris facies et non tolerabile nomen,
ire volunt, omnemque fugae perferre laborem.
sentences.l:
The very mothers now, themselves, to whom bitter once
seemed the face of the sea and the name not to be endured,
wish to go, and all the toil of flight to bear through.
sentences.i: Even the mothers now, and the very men to whom the face of the sea once seemed harsh and its name unbearable, are ready to go and to endure all the toil of flight.
sentences.n: 'Ipsae… matres, ipsi' is 'the mothers themselves, the men themselves', the emphasis on the very ones who had hated the sea (the women of 615–617). 'Quibus… visa' is 'to whom seemed', 'visa (est)' with 'aspera' predicative, 'harsh', 'maris facies' 'the face of the sea'. 'Non tolerabile nomen' is 'the unbearable name': the Latin Library prints 'numen', 'divinity', for 'nomen', 'name', a difference of sense, though both would fit the sea as a force to be feared. 'Ire volunt… perferre' is 'wish to go and to bear through', 'perferre omnem laborem' 'endure all the toil to the end', 'fugae' a genitive, 'of the flight' from Troy.

sentences.t:
Quos bonus Aeneas dictis solatur amicis,
et consanguineo lacrimans commendat Acestae.
sentences.l:
Whom good Aeneas with words kind consoles,
and to his kinsman, weeping, commends Acestes.
sentences.i: Good Aeneas comforts them with kind words, and with tears commends them to his kinsman Acestes.
sentences.n: 'Quos' is a connecting relative, 'and them' (you'll see this constantly). 'Bonus Aeneas' is 'good Aeneas', 'dictis… amicis' 'with kindly words', an ablative of means. 'Solatur' is the present of the deponent 'solor'. 'Consanguineo… Acestae' is a dative, 'to his kinsman Acestes', 'Acestae' the dative of the Greek-type name 'Acestes' (accusative 'Acesten' at 746); the kinship is that of Trojan blood. 'Lacrimans' is 'weeping', 'commendat' is 'entrusts'.

sentences.t:
Tris Eryci vitulos et Tempestatibus agnam
caedere deinde iubet, solvique ex ordine funem.
sentences.l:
Three to Eryx calves and to the Tempests a ewe lamb
to slaughter then he orders, and to be loosed in order the cable.
sentences.i: Then he orders three calves to be slain for Eryx and a ewe-lamb for the Tempests, and the cable to be cast off in order.
sentences.n: 'Tris' is Greenough's accusative plural in '-is', 'three' (you'll see this constantly). 'Eryci' is a dative, 'for Eryx', the hero and deity of the mountain, 'Tempestatibus' a dative, 'for the Tempests', the storm-powers worshipped at Rome as Tempestates. 'Caedere' and 'solvi' are infinitives after 'iubet', the second passive, 'to be loosed', with 'funem' as its subject, 'ex ordine' 'in due order', each ship in its turn. Sacrifice to storm-spirits aims to keep them calm.

sentences.t:
Ipse, caput tonsae foliis evinctus olivae,
stans procul in prora pateram tenet, extaque salsos
proiicit in fluctus ac vina liquentia fundit.
sentences.l:
Himself, his head with leaves bound of trimmed olive,
standing far off on the prow holds the bowl, and the entrails into the salt
waves casts and wine flowing pours.
sentences.i: Himself, his head wreathed with leaves of trimmed olive, standing apart on the prow he holds the bowl, flings the entrails into the salt waves, and pours out the flowing wine.
sentences.n: 'Ipse' is Aeneas himself. 'Caput… evinctus' is 'bound as to the head', 'caput' an accusative of respect, 'evinctus' the perfect participle passive of 'evincio'; 'tonsae… olivae' is 'of a trimmed olive', the olive branch used as a priest's wreath. 'Procul in prora' is 'apart on the prow', 'pateram tenet' 'holds the libation bowl'. 'Exta' are the entrails of the victims, thrown into the sea as the offering, 'salsos… in fluctus' 'into the salt waves' (the Latin Library prints 'proicit' for Greenough's 'proiicit', the same word). 'Vina liquentia' is 'liquid wine', the libation, and 'fundit' 'pours out'.

sentences.t: Prosequitur surgens a puppi ventus euntes.
sentences.l: Follows, rising from the stern, a wind them going.
sentences.i: A wind rises from astern and follows them as they go.
sentences.n: The Latin Library's text lacks this line, so the detector shows nothing to compare; Greenough prints it, unbracketed, and it is the line that brings the wind that takes the ships out. 'Prosequitur' is 'follows', 'sees off', with 'euntes' an accusative present participle, 'them going', and 'a puppi' 'from the stern', 'a following wind'. 'Surgens' is 'rising', agreeing with 'ventus'.

sentences.t: Certatim socii feriunt mare et aequora verrunt.
sentences.l: In rivalry the comrades strike the sea and the waters sweep.
sentences.i: The crews vie with one another as they beat the sea and sweep the waters.
sentences.n: 'Certatim' is 'in rivalry', each crew eager to be first. 'Feriunt mare et aequora verrunt' is 'strike the sea and sweep the levels', 'verro' ('sweep') the verb for rowing, as 'feriunt' ('strike') for the oars' blow: two ways of saying that they row with all their strength. The scene closes the Sicilian stay and leads to the open sea and Palinurus.
